haiku-low.q1: Only a SHA-256 token_hash is stored in api_tokens. Plaintext appears only in browser memory for the create dialog and the one 201 create response.
haiku-low.q2: They cannot. The full token is shown one time only and never again, not even to support. The user must create a new token.
haiku-low.q3: The create returns 422 with a message telling the user to revoke a token first. Nothing is written.
haiku-low.q4: On the first API request that starts after the revoke response returns, because each request reads the row with no cache. In-flight requests may still succeed.
haiku-low.q5: All three get the same 401 status and generic body, so the responses do not differ and reveal nothing about which check failed.
haiku-low.q6: The server computes SHA-256 of the presented token and looks up the row where token_hash matches. It is usable only if revoked_at is unset and expires_at is in the future.
haiku-low.q7: A successful authenticated API request triggers it when last_used_at is NULL or older than 15 minutes. The check uses the stored Postgres value, so it survives restarts. The doc says 15 minutes, not 1 hour.
haiku-low.q8: Nothing visible. The API response is unchanged, the error is logged without the token, and the next request retries the write.
haiku-low.q9: It sets revoked_at to now, keeping any earlier value via COALESCE. The list shows only unrevoked, unexpired rows, so the token disappears from it.
haiku-low.q10: Another user's token gives 0 rows and 404, the same as a nonexistent id. Revoking an already revoked own token keeps the first time and returns 200, since it is idempotent.
haiku-low.q11: A row is committed whose token can never be shown. It counts toward the limit and appears in the list. The user can revoke it, or it expires after 90 days; the browser must not auto-retry.

sonnet.q1: Only a SHA-256 hash (token_hash) is stored in the Postgres api_tokens table. Plaintext appears only in the 201 create response and in browser memory for the create dialog; it is never written to storage, logs or analytics.
sonnet.q2: They cannot. The token is shown only once and can never be shown again, even to support or engineers. They must create a new token (and can revoke the lost one).
sonnet.q3: The create is rejected with 422 (limit reached, revoke a token first). The transaction is rolled back and nothing is written.
sonnet.q4: On the very next request after the revoke. Each API request reads the row with no cache, so it gets 401. Requests already in flight during the revoke may still succeed.
sonnet.q5: The same 401 status with the same generic body in all cases. The responses do not differ.
sonnet.q6: The server computes SHA-256 of the presented token and selects the row WHERE token_hash matches (unique, indexed) on every request. The row is usable if it exists, revoked_at is not set, and expires_at is not in the past.
sonnet.q7: A valid API request where last_used_at is NULL or older than 15 minutes triggers a background UPDATE last_used_at = now(). The throttle compares against the last_used_at stored in Postgres. Note: the document says at most one write per 15 minutes per token, not per hour (the 1 hour is the brief's staleness allowance).
sonnet.q8: Nothing. The error is logged without the token, the API response is unchanged (the write is a background write the response does not wait for), and the next request retries the write.
sonnet.q9: It sets revoked_at = COALESCE(revoked_at, now()) on the row, so the first revoke time is kept. The row is not deleted. The list shows only rows that are not revoked and not expired, so the revoked token leaves the list.
sonnet.q10: Someone else's token (or a nonexistent id) returns 404, the same whether or not it exists, because 0 rows match id and session user. A repeat revoke of your own already-revoked token succeeds with 200 (idempotent), keeping the original revoked_at.
sonnet.q11: The row is committed and counts toward the 10-token limit, but its token can never be shown again. The browser shows an error. The row appears in the list so the user can revoke it (or it ages out after 90 days) and then create a new token. The browser must not retry automatically, since a retry would create a second token.
